title: The Velocity Deficit: Initial Energy Injection for Flow Matching
claim: The learned model systematically underestimates target magnitude, so trajectories stall short of the data and samples degrade; correcting this restores quality.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right; line plot, image comparison rows, polar trajectory diagram
description: Three panels, left to right. (a) A line plot of velocity magnitude against time from noise to data. A dashed gray line shows the roughly constant training target near 83. A blue curve for the model's prediction decays from about 65 to about 52. The gap between them is shaded gray and labeled 'Velocity Deficit'. (b) Two stacked rounded boxes of ImageNet samples. A blue box on top is labeled 'Flow Matching' and holds baseline images of a cougar, a bolo tie and a rabbit, with column labels 'Incomplete Object', 'Residual Artifacts' and 'Distorted Details'. A green box below holds cleaner images from 'Ours(SSC)'. Blue and green arrows point at the boxes. (c) A circular diagram with the noise point x0 at the center and a dashed ring for the data manifold x1. Blue baseline trajectories stop inside the ring, and green improved trajectories reach it. A double arrow marks 'Insufficient Integration'. Blue is used for the baseline and green for the proposed method throughout.
caption: The Velocity Deficit Phenomenon and Correction Strategy. (a) On ImageNet-1k 256 × 256, the learned baseline magnitude (Blue) of SiT decays monotonically, deviating from the constant OT target and creating a Velocity Deficit (Shaded Area), which represents the missing kinetic energy required for transport. (b) The velocity deficit leads to pronounced visual degradation in baseline samples, including Residual Artifacts, Incomplete Object, and Distorted Details. SSC effectively mitigates these failures by initial energy injection. (c) Standard flow matching models (Blue) fail to generate trajectories that reach the target data manifold (Black Ring), resulting in a significant Integration Lag. Our correction (Green) compensates for the signal starvation, drastically reducing this lag.
abstract: While Flow Matching theoretically guarantees constant-velocity trajectories, we identify a critical breakdown in high-dimensional practice: the Velocity Deficit. We show that the MSE objective systematically underestimates velocity magnitude, causing generated samples to fail to reach the data manifold-a phenomenon we term Integration Lag. To rectify this, we propose Initial Energy Injection, instantiated via two complementary methods: the training-based Magnitude-Aware Flow Matching (MAFM) and the training-free Scale Schedule Corrector (SSC). Both are grounded in our discovery of a crucial asymmetry: velocity contraction causes harmful kinetic stagnation at the trajectory's start, yet acts as a beneficial denoising mechanism at its end. Empirically, SSC yields significant efficiency gains with zero retraining and just one line of code. On ImageNet-1k (256x256), it improves FID by 44.6% (from 13.68 to 7.58) and achieves a 5x speedup, enabling a 50-step generator (FID 7.58) to beat a 250-step baseline (FID 8.65). Furthermore, our methods generalize to Text-to-Image tasks and high-resolution generation, improving FID on MS-COCO by ~22%.
